title: Disorder signatures in coherent electronic waveguides
abstract: Microscopic disorder in a coherent conductor is encoded in the magnitude of the transmitted current and in the energy- and channel-resolved structure of the scattering response. We develop a conductance-balanced learning framework for identifying microscopic disorder mechanisms from coherent quantum-transport spectra. Using armchair graphene nanoribbons as controlled multichannel tight-binding waveguides, we generate ensembles in which distinct disorder classes occupy the same intervals of integrated transmission, removing the dominant shortcut associated with average conductance. Within this constrained setting, we compare scalar transmission spectra with transmission-eigenvalue spectra, and use supervised classification, scale-normalizing controls, plateau-resolved tests, and principal-component analysis to identify the spectral structures that remain informative. The learned distinctions persist after normalization of the conductance envelope and are strongest in multichannel energy windows, where mode mixing and channel redistribution shape the scattering response. Principal components provide interpretable transport coordinates whose loadings identify the energy and eigenchannel sectors responsible for the dominant spectral deformations. The results establish a controlled AI-assisted protocol for learning disorder signatures from nonlinear quantum-scattering data.
summary: This paper introduces a novel, AI-driven protocol to diagnose the underlying physical mechanism of disorder in coherent electronic waveguides. By comparing detailed spectral features—specifically transmission eigenvalues rather than just average conductance—the authors show that distinct types of microscopic disorder leave unique, measurable fingerprints. This establishes a powerful metrological tool for interpreting complex quantum transport measurements.
main_problem: To develop a robust method for identifying specific microscopic disorder mechanisms within coherent electronic waveguides, overcoming the challenge that different physical disorders can yield similar average conductance.
main_result: The analysis establishes a controlled AI-assisted protocol showing that mechanism-specific fingerprints of disorder persist in the spectral shape and eigenchannel redistribution, even when total average conductance is artificially matched across different disorder classes.
method: The authors use a conductance-balanced learning framework, comparing scalar transmission spectra with transmission-eigenvalue spectra using supervised classification and Principal Component Analysis (PCA).
model_or_system: The primary model uses armchair graphene nanoribbons as controlled multi-channel tight-binding waveguides. Disorder is introduced via onsite potential variations, hopping changes, or discrete defects.
key_observables: Total transmitted weight $T(E)$, transmission eigenvalues $\{	au_n(E)\}$, and PCA loadings identifying energy/eigenchannel sectors responsible for spectral deformations.
important_parameters: Energy ($E$), disorder strength (controlled via specific mechanisms like onsite vs. hopping), and the number of active channels (multichannel regime).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on controlling the average conductance ($\langle T(E) angle$) to isolate mechanism-specific spectral features, acknowledging that a unique reconstruction from external observables is generally impossible.
figures_summary: Figures schematically illustrate the setup comparing ensemble transmission $T(E)$ versus $\langle T(E) angle$, and the core analysis involves comparing scalar vs. eigenvalue spectra using various diagnostic tools.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the physical model (disordered waveguides), then developing a controlled comparison framework (conductance balancing), applying advanced diagnostics (eigenvalue/PCA analysis), and concluding with the establishment of a general, mechanism-specific metrological protocol for quantum transport data.
why_interesting: This work bridges condensed matter theory (quantum transport in disordered systems) with modern machine learning techniques (AI-assisted pattern recognition), providing new diagnostic tools for analyzing complex many-body scattering data that might be relevant to open quantum system characterization.

FIG. 4. Transport distinguishability map for the conductance-balanced disorder ensemble. Rows denote the actual disorder mechanism and columns the predicted mech- anism. The plotted entries are row-normalized prediction probabilities, Eq. (20). Each square is split by input represen- tation: lower-left triangles use the total transmission T(E), while upper-right triangles use the transmission-eigenvalue spectra {τn(E)}. Large diagonal entries indicate disorder mechanisms whose spectra are assigned to their own class, whereas off-diagonal entries reveal disorder classes with simi- lar conductance-balanced transport responses.

FIG. 5. Spectral-shape controls for the conductance- balanced disorder ensemble. The figure compares disorder- class classification after transformations that suppress abso- lute conductance scale: raw spectra, area-normalized spec- tra, per-spectrum standardized spectra, and finite-difference spectra for the scalar transmission. Robust performance un- der area normalization and standardization indicates that the learned fingerprints are carried by spectral shape and channel redistribution rather than by average transmission.
